analysis.title: Copper some thoughts on the move... (McGeoch, FICC & Equities, 3 Nov 2026)
key_insights: Copper sold off on 3 Nov. The desk saw minimal engagement during the day. The main action was in China overnight, via CNH, a GIR link and CTA flows. McGeoch still advises using the period to lean into upside in GSXGCOPP.

Chinese shorts were added on SHFE overnight. Aggregate open interest rose 20k contracts, or 3.8%. The desk's best explanations are RMB weakness, Chinese AI weakness, a Democratic midterm sweep making Section 232 tariffs less likely, and a view that SHFE spreads cannot tighten further due to exchange focus. The desk says none of these is a good answer.

The desk argues China is too short of copper for price to collapse significantly. That would require US imports to slow with the metal redirected to China, and/or Chinese scrap VAT issues to be resolved. Neither is happening now.
Chinese inventory is at critical levels. Social plus bond stocks are -66% y/y and downstream stocks are -8% y/y. The desk expects a restocking bid as price drops.
Chinese spot (RMB, customs cleared) and CIF (USD, bonded) premiums are both near local highs as China tries to incentivise imports.
US imports remain strong. The desk estimates 260k MT for October and 180k MT for November.

Scrap is tight. The October 2026 secondary rod estimate is -53% y/y. Chinese smelters are cutting on low TCRC, and some satellite consultancies talk of a 15% sequential contraction in Chinese refined production in November.
Desk path: AI capex and Middle East escalation concerns plus a lack of tariff clarity drag copper lower given the technical break. Then price runs into a physical Chinese bid that stops the sell-off.

GIR diverges from consensus on the midterms. A Democratic House might suggest tariff rollbacks, but GIR expects President Trump to bypass legislative gridlock and announce new, broad tariff hikes after the election. That would raise the effective US tariff rate by nearly 2 percentage points.

GIR sees regulatory threats on data centers fading quickly after November. It judges a national moratorium highly unlikely and expects a lighter-touch, bipartisan AI regulatory framework focused on self-testing.
The note's setup is to lean into resilient AI infrastructure and data center names while hedging for executive-driven tariff pressure.
